The distinction matters because the two doctrines do different work: representative government legitimises the legislature and limits burdens on political communication and voting, while responsible government disciplines the executive between elections. Australia’s “Washminster” system fuses the two in practice — ministers sit in, and are drawn from, the elected Parliament.

topics.title: NSW and Commonwealth constitutional history
key_concepts: Derivation of Australian law from England: Blackstone’s three modes — conquest, cession, settlement. Australia treated as settled (Cooper v Stuart (1889) 14 App Cas 286): settlers brought so much English law as was applicable to their new situation. Reception formalised by the Australian Courts Act 1828 (Imp) (reception date 25 July 1828 for NSW); extent of reception tested by suitability (Trigwell (1979)); Imperial legislation later tidied up by the Imperial Acts Application Act 1969 (NSW).
Colonial legal development:
Early autocratic rule by Governors (prerogative; Rum Rebellion 1808).
New South Wales Act 1823 (Imp) — first Legislative Council (appointed); Supreme Court established.
Australian Courts Act 1828 (Imp) — reception of English law; court structure.
Australian Constitutions Act (No 1) 1842 (Imp) — partly elected Legislative Council.
Australian Constitutions Act (No 2) 1850 (Imp) — colonies empowered to draft their own constitutions.
NSW Constitution Act 1855 (Imp) — bicameral Parliament; responsible self-government (executive accountable to the legislature).
Colonial Laws Validity Act 1865 (Imp) — colonial laws void if repugnant to UK laws extending to the colony; confirmed colonial legislatures’ powers within limits.
Appeals to the Privy Council maintained imperial legal supervision (Phillips v Eyre (1870) — indirect repugnancy analysis).
Colonial courts and the people who ran them (1 Aug 2026 tutorial — all examinable, see B.11):
In England, judges had security of tenure from the Act of Settlement 1701. Colonial judges had none: they could be dismissed by the British government and ranked below the Governor.

Federation (1 January 1901): conventions → Commonwealth of Australia Constitution Act 1900 (Imp); six colonies became States; new federal division of powers; High Court created 1903 (s 71; Judiciary Act 1903 (Cth)).

The independence chain (lecturer: “I’ve said it 3 times — you must know it”): Balfour Declaration 1926 (dominions equal in status) → Statute of Westminster 1931 (UK) (repugnancy invalidity removed; UK laws only with dominion consent; adopted by Australia only in 1942, retrospective to 3 September 1939) → Privy Council (Limitation of Appeals) Act 1968 (Cth) and Privy Council (Appeals from the High Court) Act 1975 (Cth) → Australia Acts 1986 (Cth and UK): ended ALL appeals to the Privy Council (from State courts — the must-know point), terminated UK legislative power over Australia, and ended repugnancy restrictions and reservation of State bills; States gained full legislative power (including extraterritorial — Mobil Oil (2002)). The remaining UK link is the shared Crown.

questions.question: When and how did Australia become legally independent of the United Kingdom?
questions.answer: Answer. Independence came in stages, not at Federation. NSW began as a settled colony, so English law was received as far as applicable to colonial conditions (Cooper v Stuart (1889)), and the Australian Courts Act 1828 fixed the reception date. Colonial legislatures were subordinate. The Colonial Laws Validity Act 1865 voided colonial laws repugnant to UK statutes extending to the colony, and the Privy Council in London heard Australian appeals as the final court. Federation in 1901 created a self-governing Commonwealth, but the Constitution was itself an Act of the UK Parliament, so legal subordination continued. The Statute of Westminster 1931 removed the main restrictions on Dominion legislation, yet Australia adopted it only in 1942, backdated to 1939. Privy Council appeals were then closed step by step: limited by the Privy Council (Limitation of Appeals) Act 1968 (Cth), ended from the High Court by the Privy Council (Appeals from the High Court) Act 1975 (Cth), and finally ended from State courts by the Australia Acts 1986, passed in matching form by the Commonwealth and UK Parliaments. Those Acts also terminated any remaining UK power to legislate for Australia. So legal independence was completed only in 1986. Federation made Australia politically self-governing; adoption of the Statute of Westminster made the Commonwealth legislatively independent; the Australia Acts completed independence for the whole federation.

questions.question: Trace the development of courts and legislature in NSW from 1788 to responsible government.
questions.answer: Answer. NSW began as a penal colony ruled by a Governor whose commission allowed regulations but not legislation. Justice was military in character. A 1787 UK Act (27 Geo III c 2) created a criminal court of a Judge Advocate and six officers with no jury, and the First Charter of Justice created a civil court with appeals to the Governor and, for claims over £300, to the Privy Council. The first case, Cable v Sinclair [1788] NSWKR 7, showed that even convicts could sue. The Second Charter (1814) created the Supreme Court of NSW, and the Third Charter (1823) built a comprehensive court system, the model for today’s, plus a Legislative Council appointed by the Crown whose laws the Chief Justice had to certify as consistent with English law. The Australian Courts Act 1828 (UK) s 24 received all English law in force on 25 July 1828 and introduced trial by jury. Representative institutions grew in steps: a Legislative Council two-thirds elected from 1842; power to create bicameral parliaments in 1850; and the New South Wales Constitution Act 1855 (UK), which established the bicameral Parliament with wide domestic powers. Subordination persisted through the Colonial Laws Validity Act 1865, which voided colonial laws repugnant to UK statutes, until the Statute of Westminster 1931 (adopted by Australia in 1942) freed NSW legislation from British paramountcy. The arc runs from a Governor’s near-absolute power to representative, responsible and legislatively independent government.

topics.title: NSW and Commonwealth Constitutions compared
key_concepts: NSW Constitution: principal source now the Constitution Act 1902 (NSW) (consolidating the 1855 (Imp) Act tradition). Unlike the Commonwealth’s single entrenched document, it is flexible — mostly amendable by ordinary legislation (McCawley v The King (1920) 28 CLR 106), except manner-and-form entrenched provisions such as s 7A.
NSW structure — Crown and Governor:

ss 3, 8A, 9A Constitution Act 1902 (NSW) + Australia Act 1986 (Imp) ss 7–10: the Governor is the King’s representative in NSW (s 9A; Australia Act s 7(1)); the Premier advises the King directly on State matters; no more UK oversight — Australia Act ss 8–10 ended the reservation of State bills, UK legislative power and repugnancy invalidity.

Executive in practice: Governor, Premier and Ministers; the Executive Council formalises Cabinet decisions (ss 35B–35D); reserve powers and responsible-government conventions mirror the Commonwealth level (executive accountable to the Assembly).
NSW structure — Legislative Council (upper house):

s 7 (constitution), s 17 (election), s 22B(2): 42 members elected by state-wide proportional representation for eight-year staggered terms — half the Council faces election every four years at a general election. It is a continuing body — not subject to dissolution (stability/institutional memory).

Manner-and-form entrenchment (CLVA 1865 tradition): s 7A — the Council cannot be abolished, and s 7A itself cannot be amended, without a referendum. Enforced in Attorney-General (NSW) v Trethowan [1932] AC 526 — a law passed in breach of a manner-and-form requirement is invalid; the CLVA 1865 supplied the authority for such self-entrenchment. Courts enforce compliance with manner-and-form requirements.

Clayton v Heffron (1960) 105 CLR 214 — the s 7A referendum protects the Council even against the s 5B deadlock route: an abolition Bill must itself pass both Houses before going to the people, so the Assembly and Executive cannot use the deadlock machinery to bypass the Council.
NSW structure — Legislative Assembly (lower house):

s 24: four-year term running from the return of the writs. Fixed four-year terms introduced by the Constitution Amendment (Fixed Term Parliaments) Act 1995 (NSW); the Governor retains power to dissolve early (on advice); extending the term requires a referendum (s 7B).
Rationale for the different terms: the Assembly gives frequent elections and direct voter accountability; the Council gives continuity and review.

Relationship between the NSW Houses — deadlock machinery: ss 5A, 5B Constitution Act 1902 (NSW) set deadlock procedures where the Council rejects Assembly bills (joint sittings etc.); Clayton v Heffron protects the Council within that machinery; Taylor v Attorney-General (Qld) (1917) 23 CLR 457 on money bills and upper houses.

NSW legislative power is plenary, not enumerated: s 5 Constitution Act 1902 (NSW) — laws “for the peace, welfare and good government of New South Wales”, words of the widest amplitude (Union Steamship Co of Australia Pty Ltd v King (1988) 166 CLR 1); extraterritorial competence confirmed by the Australia Acts 1986 (Mobil Oil (2002)). Constraints: the Commonwealth Constitution (ss 90, 92, 109, 114–117) and Ch III (Kable). “Plenary power” is “a particular favourite of examiners the country over” — contrast the Commonwealth’s enumerated heads.

s 109 doctrine in full (updated Topic 12 slides — high-yield): confirms Commonwealth supremacy over concurrent powers; operates only where both laws are otherwise valid; “invalid” means inoperative, not void — the State law revives if the Commonwealth law is repealed (Carter v Egg and Egg Pulp Marketing Board (1942) 66 CLR 557 per Latham CJ). Tests of “real conflict”: (1) direct — impossibility of simultaneous obedience; (2) direct — one law alters, impairs or detracts from a right, privilege or immunity conferred by the other; (3) indirect — “cover the field” (Ex parte McLean (1930) 43 CLR 472; Viskauskas v Niland (1983) 153 CLR 280).

Stott v Commonwealth [2025] HCA 39 (decided 15 October 2025) — the essential 2025 case: Vic/Qld foreign-owner land tax/duty surcharges were inconsistent with non-discrimination clauses in Australia’s tax treaties (given domestic force by the International Tax Agreements Act 1953 (Cth)) — “an exemplar of the application of s 109”. The HCA unanimously upheld the Commonwealth’s retrospective cure (Treasury Laws Amendment (Foreign Investment) Act 2024 (Cth)) and overruled Metwally as “manifestly wrong”. Takeaway: the Commonwealth can now retrospectively remove s 109 inconsistency and revive State laws.

Executive government (Topic 13 lecture): s 61 vests executive power in the Crown, exercisable by the G-G, extending to the “execution and maintenance of this Constitution, and of the laws of the Commonwealth”; content includes the prerogatives appropriate to the Commonwealth’s spheres (Davis (1988); Ruddock v Vadarlis (2001) — the Tampa case) and a nationhood dimension (AAP Case (1975)). Limits: Pape v FCT (2009) (national-crisis spending); Williams [2012] HCA 23 — no spending/contracting without statutory authority merely because s 51 would support a law; displacement by statute requires clear words (De Keyser’s (1920)). Cabinet operates by convention (Peko-Wallsend); responsible government means an executive accountable to Parliament (ministerial responsibility, though weakened in modern practice).

questions.question: Compare the NSW Constitution with the Commonwealth Constitution.
questions.answer: Answer. The two constitutions are different in kind. The Commonwealth Constitution is a single entrenched document. It can be amended only by the s 128 double-majority referendum, it grants enumerated powers (ss 51–52), and it is supreme: laws inconsistent with it are invalid. The NSW Constitution is mainly the Constitution Act 1902 (NSW), a flexible statute amendable by ordinary legislation. McCawley (1920) confirmed that State parliaments are not generally bound by manner-and-form requirements they have not enacted. Instead of enumerated heads, s 5 grants plenary power to make laws “for the peace, welfare and good government” of the State. On separation of powers, NSW has none in the strict sense (Gilbertson v South Australia), while the Commonwealth separates judicial power strictly through Chapter III. Yet the NSW Constitution has real constitutional force in three ways. Manner-and-form entrenchment: s 7A requires a referendum to abolish the Legislative Council, and the courts enforce it (Trethowan (1931), where an injunction restrained presenting a Bill for assent without one). Federal supremacy: ss 90 and 109 of the Commonwealth Constitution bind NSW at every point. And Kable (1996): NSW cannot legislate to impair the institutional integrity of its courts, because they form part of the federal judicature. In short, NSW chose flexible, UK-style constitutionalism inside a federation, while the Commonwealth chose entrenchment and enumeration. The NSW system works only because the federal framework disciplines it.

questions.question: Compare the two Houses of the NSW Parliament with the Commonwealth Houses — composition, terms and deadlocks.
questions.answer: Answer. Both Parliaments are bicameral, but each level builds its houses on different logic. In NSW, the Legislative Assembly has 93 members from single-member districts serving fixed four-year terms running from the return of the writs (s 24, Constitution Act 1902 (NSW), fixed by the 1995 amendment). The Governor can dissolve it early on advice, but the term cannot be extended without a referendum (s 7B). The Legislative Council has 42 members elected by state-wide proportional representation for eight-year staggered terms, half facing each general election (s 22B(2)). It is a continuing body that is never dissolved, and s 7A entrenches it: abolition needs a referendum (Trethowan). The design trades accountability in the lower house against stability and institutional memory in the upper. At the Commonwealth level, the House of Representatives is elected from single-member divisions for a maximum of three years (s 28), and the nexus clause (s 24) keeps it as near as practicable twice the Senate’s size. The Senate gives the original States equal representation with six-year rotating terms (ss 7, 13), and the Territorial Senators Cases (1975 and 1977) upheld territory senators under s 122. Money Bills are privileged to the lower house (ss 53–55). The deadlock machinery differs too. The Commonwealth uses s 57: double dissolution, then a joint sitting, strictly applied (PMA Case (1975)). NSW uses ss 5A–5B: a free conference, then a referendum, which cannot be used to sidestep the Council where manner-and-form protections apply (Clayton v Heffron (1960) 105 CLR 214; compare Taylor v A-G (Qld) (1917) 23 CLR 457).

questions.question: What is the “cover the field” test of s 109 inconsistency, and how has it been applied — including the 2025 development?
questions.answer:
Answer. Cover the field is the indirect test of s 109 inconsistency. Section 109 provides that where a State law is inconsistent with a Commonwealth law, the Commonwealth law prevails and the State law is, to the extent of the inconsistency, inoperative — not void: if the Commonwealth law were repealed, the State law revives (Carter v Egg and Egg Pulp Marketing Board (1942) per Latham CJ). s 109 operates only where both laws are otherwise valid.

Direct tests ask whether simultaneous obedience is impossible, or whether one law alters, impairs or detracts from a right conferred by the other. The indirect “cover the field” test asks instead whether the Commonwealth law evinces an intention to be a complete, exhaustive or exclusive statement of the law on the subject; if so, any State law on that subject is inconsistent, even though obedience to both is possible (Ex parte McLean (1930)). In Viskauskas v Niland (1983) the Racial Discrimination Act 1975 (Cth) occupied the field of racial discrimination, leaving the State Anti-Discrimination Act inoperative.

University of Wollongong v Metwally (1984) had held that Parliament could not retrospectively cure a s 109 inconsistency. Stott v Commonwealth [2025] HCA 39 — “an exemplar of the application of s 109” — overruled Metwally as “manifestly wrong”: State foreign-owner tax surcharges were inconsistent with non-discrimination clauses in Australia’s tax treaties, and the High Court unanimously upheld the Commonwealth’s retrospective validating Act. The Commonwealth can now remove s 109 inconsistency retrospectively and revive State laws.

topics.title: Courts and tribunals
key_concepts: Judicial power and separation: federal judicial power only in Ch III courts; State courts may be invested with federal jurisdiction (s 77(ii)–(iii)) but then must meet Ch III institutional-integrity standards (Kable).
Federal hierarchy:

High Court of Australia — apex; original jurisdiction ss 75 (mandamus/prohibition/injunction against Commonwealth officers — s 75(v); treaties; inter-State/Commonwealth disputes) and 76; appellate s 73 (from federal courts and State supreme courts — one common law: Lipohar). 7 Justices: High Court of Australia Act 1979 (Cth) s 6.
Federal Court of Australia (1976) — corporations, industrial, migration, native title, trade practices; Full Court appeals.
Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia (FCFCOA) — since 1 September 2021 (merger of Family Court and Federal Circuit Court; Division 1 appeals/complex, Division 2 general).
State/Territory Supreme Courts exercising federal jurisdiction; cross-vesting scheme between federal/State supreme courts.

Cross-vesting limits — Re Wakim; Ex parte McNally (1999) 198 CLR 511: the Commonwealth can invest State courts with federal jurisdiction, but the States cannot confer State jurisdiction on federal courts (Ch III forbids) — the cross-vesting scheme survives only in the State-to-federal direction.
NSW hierarchy:
Supreme Court of NSW (unlimited civil jurisdiction; Equity and Common Law Divisions; Court of Appeal and Court of Criminal Appeal) — Supreme Court Act 1970 (NSW).
District Court of NSW — intermediate (civil to ~$1.25m; indictable crime; limited equitable jurisdiction — lecturer’s point: know where to file).
Local Court of NSW — summary crime, small civil claims, committals.
Specialist: Land and Environment Court, Children’s Court, Coroner’s Court, Drug Court; Industrial Relations Commission.

What is a court / judicial power (Week 12 lecture): the label is irrelevant — the question is whether the body exercises judicial power (Lane v Morrison (2009) 239 CLR 230: the Australian Military Court, on fixed terms and inside the defence command structure, was invalid). Judicial power determines rights and liabilities conclusively and enforceably (Huddart Parker (1909); Totani (2010) per Kiefel J); it is coercive, in invitum — unlike consensual arbitral power, which creates new rights (Waterside Workers (1918); TCL Air (2013)). Independence and impartiality are essential to any body exercising judicial power (Gypsy Jokers (2008)). Characterisation is contextual — no exhaustive definition is possible (Precision Data (1991)).

Boilermakers’ Case (R v Kirby; Ex parte Boilermakers’ Society (1956) 94 CLR 254) — strict separation at the federal level: a Ch III court cannot exercise non-judicial power, and non-judicial tribunals cannot exercise federal judicial power (the dual judicial/arbitral Arbitration Court was invalidly constituted; upheld by the Privy Council). Exceptions: persona designata functions (Hilton v Wells (1985)); administrative functions incidental to judicial functions (Harris v Caladine (1991)). Burns v Corbett (2018) 265 CLR 304 — a State tribunal (NCAT) cannot exercise federal judicial power (e.g. s 75(iv) diversity matters).

Jurisdiction (Week 12): the authority of a court to hear and decide the matter before it (Harris v Caladine); when properly invoked, it must be exercised. Original vs appellate — appellate jurisdiction is a creature of statute; there is no common law right of appeal (e.g. Supreme Court Act 1970 (NSW) s 101). Supervisory jurisdiction: the Supreme Court keeps inferior courts, tribunals and decision-makers within lawful power (mandamus, prohibition, certiorari) and it cannot be excluded — Kirk (2010); jurisdictional errors vs errors within jurisdiction — Craig (1995); jurisdictional error reviewable despite finality clauses — Probuild (2018). Federal jurisdiction needs a justiciable “matter” — no advisory opinions; accrued/associated jurisdiction (s 32 FCA Act; Philip Morris) covers State-law claims sharing a “common substratum of facts” with the federal claim.

Tribunals and administrative review: tribunals are not Ch III courts — they conduct merits review (the “correct and preferable” decision on the facts, law and policy; Drake (1979)) and cannot exercise judicial power (Boilermakers). Federal: the Administrative Review Tribunal (ART) replaced the AAT on 14 October 2024; National Native Title Tribunal. NSW: NCAT (from 2014 — consumer, tenancy, guardianship, administrative review). Judicial review is legality only: ADJR Act 1977 (Cth); Judiciary Act 1903 (Cth) s 39B; Constitution s 75(v) — entrenched, so removing it needs a s 128 referendum.

ADR (March 2026 Q2(a) module): negotiation; mediation (a neutral facilitates — no imposed outcome); conciliation (neutral plays a more active advisory role); expert appraisal/determination; arbitration (determinative — binding award, confidential, much harder to challenge than a judgment; courts enforce arbitration clauses). Court-connected ADR is standard case management: a NSW court may refer proceedings to mediation without the parties’ consent (Civil Procedure Act 2005 (NSW) s 26; arbitration with consent, s 38; overriding purpose of just, quick and cheap resolution, s 56) — but it cannot force settlement; the right to an adjudicated outcome remains. Over 95% of civil matters settle. Debate: settlement pressure vs the judiciary’s constitutional function of open, reasoned adjudication (Windeyer, prescribed reading).

questions.question: Why does Chapter III of the Commonwealth Constitution matter to State courts?
questions.answer: Answer. Chapter III matters to State courts because State courts exercise federal jurisdiction. Section 77(iii) lets Parliament invest State courts with federal jurisdiction, appeals run from State Supreme Courts to the High Court under s 73, and the Judiciary Act 1903 (Cth) in fact vests State courts with federal jurisdiction across the board. Once State courts form part of that integrated federal judicature, Kable v DPP (NSW) (1996) holds that State parliaments cannot pass laws impairing their institutional integrity as courts. In Kable itself, a NSW Act directed at one named prisoner was invalid because it enlisted the Supreme Court in a function incompatible with its integrity; the court was turned into an instrument of the executive. Later cases such as Fardon and Totani confirmed and refined the doctrine. The significance is easiest to see by contrast. NSW has no strict separation of judicial power for its own purposes (Gilbertson), so without Chapter III a State parliament could hand judicial functions to the executive, or non-judicial functions to courts, at will. Chapter III sets a federal floor beneath which no State parliament may go. In the wider system, the hierarchy runs from the High Court at the apex through the federal courts and the NSW courts (Supreme, District, Local), with tribunals, the federal Administrative Review Tribunal and NCAT in NSW, reviewing administrative decisions on the merits without exercising judicial power.

questions.question: The (fictional) Building Justice Act 2026 (NSW) creates a Building Disputes Tribunal (BDT) to “finally and bindingly determine” building disputes, including between residents of different States; BDT members hold renewable three-year contracts and are removable by the Minister at will. The Act also empowers a NSW Supreme Court judge, acting in a personal capacity, to make building work prohibition orders without giving reasons. Meanwhile the (fictional) Defence Housing Act 2026 (Cth) creates a “Defence Housing Court” of serving ADF officers on fixed seven-year terms to make binding determinations of housing entitlements. Advise on the constitutional validity of each determination.
questions.answer:
Answer. The interstate dispute before the BDT is a matter “between residents of different States” within s 75(iv) — federal jurisdiction. The judicial power of the Commonwealth may be exercised only by Chapter III courts (s 71; Boilermakers), and a State tribunal that is not a court of a State cannot exercise it: Burns v Corbett (2018) 265 CLR 304 (NCAT). Determining disputes “finally and bindingly” is judicial power (Lane v Morrison at [21]–[22]), and members on renewable contracts removable at ministerial will lack the independence and impartiality essential to a court (Gypsy Jokers at [10]) — the label cannot save it. The BDT therefore cannot validly determine the interstate dispute; it must go to a State or federal court. Purely intra-State matters may still be determined as an exercise of State administrative power.

The prohibition-order power is invalid under the Kable principle. State courts may be vested with non-judicial functions, but not functions incompatible with their institutional integrity as repositories of federal jurisdiction (Kable (1996); Forge v ASIC (2006)). Wainohu v NSW (2011) 243 CLR 181 is on all fours: control orders made by Supreme Court judges in a personal capacity, without reasons, were invalid — the public could not distinguish the judicial and non-judicial roles, and the absence of reasons struck at a hallmark of judicial power. The prohibition orders mirror Wainohu (reinforce with Condon v Pompano (2013) and Totani).

The Defence Housing Court is invalid. A body that determines rights and liabilities conclusively and bindingly exercises judicial power (Totani at [444] per Kiefel J), which at the federal level may be vested only in a Ch III court. Fixed seven-year terms, serving ADF officers and a command-structure location are precisely the defects that invalidated the Australian Military Court in Lane v Morrison (2009) 239 CLR 230. Calling the body a “court” makes no difference; the determination is of no effect.

questions.question: What was the significance of R v Kirby; Ex parte Boilermakers’ Society of Australia (1956) 94 CLR 254?
questions.answer:
Answer. Boilermakers established the strict separation of judicial power at the federal level — the lecturer calls it one of the most significant Australian constitutional decisions. The Commonwealth Court of Conciliation and Arbitration combined arbitral functions (making new awards — non-judicial) with judicial functions (enforcing awards). The High Court held, and the Privy Council affirmed, that Chapter III means what it says: a court exercising the judicial power of the Commonwealth cannot also be vested with non-judicial power, and a body that is not a Ch III court cannot exercise federal judicial power. The dual body was therefore invalidly constituted.

Two qualifications keep the doctrine workable. Judges may perform non-judicial functions in their personal capacity (persona designata — Hilton v Wells (1985)), and administrative functions incidental to judicial functions are permitted (Harris v Caladine (1991)).

Boilermakers also explains adjacent doctrine: federal tribunals such as the ART can conduct merits review precisely because they exercise no judicial power, and State tribunals cannot exercise federal judicial power at all (Burns v Corbett (2018)). At State level there is no strict separation (Gilbertson), but the Kable principle protects the institutional integrity of State courts as repositories of federal jurisdiction. In an exam, use Boilermakers as the anchor for any question on what makes a body a court, the content of judicial power, or the validity of hybrid tribunals.

questions.question: Distinguish mediation, arbitration and conciliation, and explain the courts’ power to compel ADR in NSW.
questions.answer:
Answer. All three are ADR processes — consensual, confidential and party-controlled alternatives (or adjuncts) to adjudication — but the neutral’s role differs. In mediation the neutral facilitates negotiation between the parties and imposes no outcome; settlement, if any, is the parties’ own and is embodied in an enforceable deed of settlement. In conciliation the neutral plays a more active, advisory role, suggesting possible terms of settlement. In arbitration the neutral hears evidence and argument and makes a binding determination — the closest process to adjudication, though consensual in origin; awards are confidential, enforceable, and much harder to challenge than a judgment, and courts will hold parties to arbitration clauses they agreed to.

Court-connected ADR is now standard case management. Under the Civil Procedure Act 2005 (NSW) a court may refer proceedings to mediation without the parties’ consent where it considers the circumstances appropriate (s 26), and to arbitration with consent (s 38); the overriding purpose of the just, quick and cheap resolution of disputes (s 56) informs those powers. Parties referred to mediation must participate in good faith — but the court cannot make them settle; the right to an adjudicated outcome always remains.

The framing point: ADR complements rather than replaces adjudication. Over 95% of civil matters settle, which serves access to justice, but courts remain essential for the authoritative, public declaration of rights (rule of law).

questions.question: Distinguish merits review from judicial review, giving the principal avenues for each.
questions.answer:
Answer. Merits review asks whether the correct and preferable decision was made on the facts, the law and policy. The reviewer stands in the shoes of the original decision-maker and may substitute a new decision (Drake v Minister for Immigration and Ethnic Affairs (1979)). It is conducted by tribunals, not courts: externally by the Administrative Review Tribunal federally (the ART replaced the AAT on 14 October 2024) and NCAT in New South Wales, or internally within the agency. Watch the legislation at every step — internal-review prerequisites, strict time limits, and leave to proceed out of time.

Judicial review asks a narrower question: was the decision lawful? The court examines legality, not merits — jurisdictional error, breach of procedural fairness, errors of law. Principal avenues: the Administrative Decisions (Judicial Review) Act 1977 (Cth) for most Commonwealth decisions; Judiciary Act 1903 (Cth) s 39B in the Federal Court; and Constitution s 75(v) in the High Court, which is entrenched — removing it would require a s 128 referendum. In NSW, judicial review operates mainly at common law through the Supreme Court’s supervisory jurisdiction (mandamus, prohibition, certiorari), which the legislature cannot exclude: Kirk (2010); Craig (1995) distinguishes jurisdictional errors (reviewable) from errors within jurisdiction (generally not); Probuild (2018) confirms review survives legislative finality clauses.

The distinction matters because it allocates work between the branches: tribunals re-decide; courts police legal limits. The lecturer’s warning: “you can’t get out of law school without knowing what merits review is”.

topics.title: Legal profession and ethics
key_concepts: The profession: fused-in-practice but functionally divided — solicitors (advise clients, prepare matters, may appear in lower courts) and barristers (specialist advocacy and advice; briefed by solicitors; the Bar). Admission via the Legal Profession Admission Board (LPAB) — academic (Priestley 11) + practical requirements (Legal Profession Uniform Admission Rules 2015, esp. r 10).

Legal ethics — core obligations: honesty and candour to the court; competence and diligence; confidentiality/legal professional privilege; avoiding conflicts of interest; civility; no misleading conduct (Solicitors’ Conduct Rules 2015 rr 2–6, 7–12, 17, 19; Barristers Rules 2015 rr 4, 8, 11–13, 17, 23). Character matters at admission and in practice — see the fitness and discipline cases (Clyne; Cummins; Re Liveri).

AI and legal practice (March 2026 Q3 theme): disruptive potential — drafting, research, prediction; risks — hallucinated citations filed with courts, confidentiality breaches via public tools, competence/verification and supervision duties, misleading the court. Lecturer’s rule of thumb: using generative AI on client work needs (1) the client’s consent and (2) your insurer’s consent.

Regulation: Legal Profession Uniform Law (NSW) — admission and practising certificates (ss 16, 17), trust accounts, conduct rules, discipline (s 419); Legal Profession Uniform Law Australian Solicitors’ Conduct Rules 2015; Legal Profession Uniform Conduct (Barristers) Rules 2015 — including the cab-rank rule: a barrister must accept a brief in their area of practice regardless of personal views about the client or cause, subject to exceptions such as conflict or inadequate fee.

The “Grand Bargain”: in exchange for monopoly, status and self-regulation, the profession accepts duties to the court and the administration of justice paramount over the duty to the client, high ethical standards, and service to the public (Brennan, ‘Profession or Service Industry: The Choice’ (1996)).

Fitness and discipline cases (examinable list): Clyne v NSW Bar Association (1960) 104 CLR 186 (striking off; “suitable person” to remain on the roll); NSW Bar Association v Cummins (2001) 52 NSWLR 279 and Hamman [1999] NSWCA 404 (fit and proper person; candour with the regulator); re OG, a lawyer [2007] VSC 520 (conduct outside practice can still demonstrate unfitness); Re Liveri [2006] QCA 152 (law-school plagiarism → admission refused); Re Humzy-Hancock [2007] QSC 34 (academic misconduct and disclosure on admission).

The judiciary: federal appointment, tenure and independence — s 72 Constitution (tenure/salary protection; removal only by address of both Houses); NSW — Judicial Officers Act 1986 (NSW) s 41 (removal only by address on proved misbehaviour/incapacity; complaints via the Conduct Division). Judicial independence underpins the rule of law — impartiality, security of tenure, freedom from executive interference, institutional integrity (Kable line).

Judicial impartiality and bias (ALRC Report 138, Without Fear or Favour, December 2021): two rules — actual bias and apprehended bias; the apprehended-bias test is objective (Ebner v Official Trustee in Bankruptcy (2000) 205 CLR 337 at [6]): would a fair-minded lay observer reasonably apprehend that the judge might not bring an impartial mind to the question? Charisteas v Charisteas (2021) — undisclosed social contact between the trial judge and a party’s barrister during the hearing → retrial ordered. ALRC: the substantive law needs no amendment, but procedures do (published disqualification protocols, an independent complaints body, transparent appointments).

Judicial independence and the rule of law (March 2026 Q3(a)): independence safeguards impartial adjudication between citizen and state; threats — executive pressure, ad hominem legislation (Kable), funding, appointments processes, public attacks; safeguards — s 72 tenure, separation of powers, convention, professional culture. Engage critically: independence is instrumental, not an end — it serves impartial justice and public confidence.

questions.question: “Artificial intelligence will not change what is owed to the court and the client — only how it is discharged.” Discuss.
questions.answer: Answer. I agree with that statement. The core duties do not change. The duty to the court comes first: candour, and never misleading. Then the duties to the client: competence, diligence, confidentiality. The profession enforces these seriously. In Re Liveri [2006] QCA 152, academic dishonesty defeated an application for admission because honesty goes to fitness to practise. AI changes none of it. A lawyer who files invented authorities generated by an AI tool misleads the court exactly as much as one who invents them personally, and courts in Australia and overseas have already disciplined lawyers for filing hallucinated citations. What changes is how the duties are discharged. Competence now includes verifying AI output before relying on it: checking that every cited case exists and says what is claimed. Confidentiality means not feeding client material into external AI systems without authority. The lecturer’s working rule was that using AI on client work requires the client’s consent and the professional indemnity insurer’s consent. Supervision extends to machine output just as it extends to a junior lawyer’s draft; the senior lawyer remains responsible for everything filed. So AI shifts the lawyer’s work from producing documents to verifying them, and that raises the standard of care rather than lowering it. The obligations are the constant. The technology is simply the new context in which the same obligations have to be honoured.

questions.question: How does the cab-rank rule apply to barristers in NSW, and what limits exist?
questions.answer:
Answer. The cab-rank rule requires a barrister to accept a brief in their area of practice regardless of their personal views about the client or the cause. It is embodied in the Legal Profession Uniform Conduct (Barristers) Rules 2015 and reflects the structure of the divided profession: solicitors brief barristers, who supply specialist advocacy and advice at the Bar.

The rule serves the administration of justice in two ways. It guarantees that even unpopular clients and causes can obtain specialist representation, and it protects the barrister’s independence — the advocate is not identified with the client’s cause, which in turn supports the profession’s paramount duty to the court. It is part of the “Grand Bargain”: in exchange for monopoly, status and self-regulation, the profession accepts duties to the court and the public ahead of its own preferences.

The rule is not absolute. A barrister may — indeed must — decline a brief where an exception applies, such as a conflict of interest or an inadequate fee. Within those limits, personal distaste for the client, the crime or the politics of the matter is no answer to a brief.

Exam angle: link the rule to the solicitor–barrister division, the paramount duty to the court, and the fitness cases (Clyne; Cummins) that police the ethical standards on which the Bargain depends.

topics.title: Exam-day briefing & lecturer flags
key_concepts: Format (September 2026, confirmed in the Week 12 lecture): five questions on the paper; answer FOUR; 20 marks each; marked out of 80. 15 minutes reading/planning + ~45 minutes per question (≈ 3 h 15 min). Only your first four UNcrossed-out answers are marked — a crossed-out attempt does not count, and effort on a fifth question is entirely wasted.

Timing: choose your four questions during reading time and note every sub-part. Write a timing plan on paper and obey it (for a 9:00 start: Q1 9:15, Q2 10:00, Q3 10:45, Q4 11:30, finish 12:15). When a question’s time is up, move on — it is much harder to push an answer from 16 to 17 than to pick up the first marks of the next question. Expect to write ~1,000 words/hour (~200–250 words per page); leaving a question half-done is the single most common cause of failure.

If caught short mid-answer: switch to dot points setting out where the answer was going — the cases, legislation and issues you would have dealt with — leave a couple of pages, write “PTO”, and come back at the end if time allows.

What the examiner rewards (March 2026 Examiner’s Comments): a clear thesis introduced up front; critical engagement with the actual question — including rejecting a provocative proposition and arguing a substantiated counter-position; every component of multi-pronged questions answered; several accurate authorities from the course materials; red herrings identified and dismissed; full sentences and paragraphs — never pure point form.

What gets penalised: reproducing prepared notes uncritically (over-reliance on the open-book format); copying word-for-word without acknowledgment; conclusions asserted without reasoned analysis or authority; citing no provision or case on point; misstating what cases stand for; conflating the approaches to statutory interpretation; irrelevant material; unanswered question-parts.

Open-book discipline: a pile of notes “will do you no good” — distil your material so you can marshal it; use the pack to locate authority fast, then answer the precise question asked. Coverage insurance: the lecturer cannot cover everything — have at least one or two sentences on each item in every topic. Keep 5 minutes per question to re-read your answer against the question asked (kill regurgitation).

Citation: formal AGLC4 is NOT required in the exam — but do identify the legislation (name + section) and the case (name + year). Underline case names and legislation so the marker can see where to look on the page, and write as clearly as you possibly can.

Problem questions: the representation in the facts will be deliberately vague — argue whether it suffices and map both branches (“maybe, maybe not — if, if not”). Always check defined terms (e.g. “person”) in the relevant interpretation Act (“in the examination you would 100% go back and talk about person”). Identify the correct client, the correct entity to sue, and the correct court before advising.

Lecturer’s must-know flags (Parts B): Blackstone, Commentaries on the Laws of England (1765–69); the Judicature Acts 1873–75; the four schools of jurisprudence (characterise each); context and purpose considered at the first stage (CIC Insurance; SZTAL); the division of powers (ss 51, 52, 90, 107, 109); separation of powers (“learn it properly and regurgitate it”); s 75(v) mandamus/prohibition; the reception date (25 July 1828); the Australia Act 1986 ended Privy Council appeals (“I’ve said it 3 times”); the maxims of equity; “plenary power” (s 5 Constitution Act 1902 (NSW)) — “a particular favourite of examiners the country over”; merits review vs judicial review; Boilermakers; the Kable ingredients (independence/impartiality, procedural fairness, open justice, the duty to give reasons).

Likely September 2026 hotspots: statutory interpretation (every year); precedent/dissent/judicial law-making; native title including Commonwealth v Yunupingu [2025] HCA 6; s 109 inconsistency including Stott v Commonwealth [2025] HCA 39; executive power (Pape; Williams — the new Topic 13 lecture); reserve powers; separation of powers and Kable; what makes a body a “court” and the content of judicial power (Lane v Morrison; Boilermakers; Burns v Corbett); merits review vs judicial review and supervisory jurisdiction (Kirk; Craig; Probuild); ADR; the legal profession and AI; definitional pairs.

NOT needed: the warm-up cases (e.g. Thornton v Shoe Lane Parking — “you don’t need to have a summary of Thornton”); the Sale of Goods Act (“don’t write that in your exam”); Wikipedia (“don’t quote Wikipedia in exams or assignments”).

Answer structure per question: one-sentence thesis up front → issue-by-issue analysis with case/section authority → counter-argument → conclusion. For definitional pairs: synthesise similarities and differences, and always end with one sentence on why the distinction matters.

Logistics: the exam is held in the city, not on campus — confirm exactly where the room is, plan parking/transport, and go and look at the room before exam day. Bring an annotated copy of the Constitution — you will have to refer to it. Print the pack double-sided and tab Parts A–E for the fastest access.
